Cybersecurity · Agentic AI · Business risk

AI Is Now Both the Weapon and the Defence. Is Your Business Ready?

$6.34 billion in digital assets affected in a Binance security incident. Customer credentials, password hashes and live tokens exposed in a separate breach at Chainalysis. Recent attacks show why businesses must rethink how they protect people, data and connected systems.

Neural Horizons AI Editorial · 8 November 2026 · 8 min read

On this pageBinanceChainalysisAI platformsFinancial-sector threatsAI as defenceQuestions for leadersSources

These are not isolated technology stories. They are warnings about the vulnerabilities created when people, data, applications and increasingly autonomous AI systems become interconnected.

Cybersecurity is entering a new phase. The question is no longer simply whether an organisation has a firewall, antivirus software or a security team. It is whether it understands who and what can access its systems, how those connections are being used and what happens when one of them is compromised.

Binance: When a trusted employee becomes the entry point

In an incident disclosed in early November, Binance reported that approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets had been affected. The company said around $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted in its initial update. Binance also said it would absorb the impact rather than pass it on to customers, and reported that affected assets had been replenished.

The company described a multi-stage campaign involving social engineering, compromised developer devices, malicious software, stolen credentials and misuse of an internal AI tool. A reported entry point involved a fake recruitment process that persuaded an engineer to download a malicious coding assignment.

The significance is not simply the scale of the incident. It is how the attackers combined human trust, compromised devices, credentials and connected technology to reach critical systems. The available reporting does not establish that an autonomous AI agent independently planned or executed the attack.

“We need to rethink what we mean by an organisation's security perimeter. It is no longer simply the network, the firewall or the physical office. It extends to every employee, every connected application, every third-party relationship and every AI-enabled workflow. A single compromised identity, combined with excessive permissions, can create consequences far beyond the original point of entry.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

That lesson extends well beyond cryptocurrency. Any business with interconnected systems, external suppliers, cloud applications and employees using AI tools needs to understand where its vulnerabilities sit.

Read Binance's incident report.

Chainalysis: When the intelligence provider becomes the target

A separate incident at blockchain intelligence company Chainalysis brought another dimension of the threat into view. The company disclosed an external attack involving what it described as offensive agentic techniques. Subsequent reporting said customer information exposed in the incident included usernames, password hashes and live tokens.

Chainalysis temporarily restricted some services while investigating and strengthening its systems. The company said it found no evidence that investigation data or its attribution intelligence had been manipulated. The precise attack path and the role played by the agentic techniques have not been fully detailed publicly.

“Data security cannot be treated as an isolated IT responsibility. Data is an organisation's commercial intelligence, its customer relationships, its intellectual property and, ultimately, its trust. As businesses introduce AI agents and connect more systems, they must understand exactly where information resides, how it moves, who can access it and what happens when one connection is compromised.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

Data is not simply something stored in a database. It is connected to people, applications, permissions, transactions and business decisions. When those connections are compromised, the consequences can extend well beyond the original system.

Read the Chainalysis incident coverage.

AI platforms are becoming part of the attack surface

A further warning came from Botpress, which disclosed unauthorised access involving an internal authentication proxy and employee API credentials. The company said bot configurations in 16 customer workspaces were accessed. Those configurations could contain third-party credentials, including AI provider keys, messaging tokens and CRM credentials.

Botpress said it had no evidence that end-user conversations or its source code had been accessed. The incident nevertheless illustrates a risk that is easy to overlook: the security of an AI application depends not only on the model, but also on the integrations, credentials and business systems connected to it.

Read Botpress's incident disclosure.

AI-assisted attacks move closer to financial infrastructure

India's cybersecurity agency CERT-In warned of an active campaign targeting non-bank lenders, fintech businesses and cryptocurrency exchanges. Reporting described the use of publicly available AI-assisted tools to automate parts of intrusion activity and target payment and disbursement systems.

Reuters also reported approximately $2 million in unauthorised transfers at two Indian lenders in a separate incident involving payment APIs. The agency did not establish that those transfers were connected to the campaign it described. That distinction matters: the incidents should not be presented as one confirmed attack.

Read the Reuters report.

Meanwhile, SecurityWeek reported a wider wave of attacks targeting AI developer platforms, with credentials and access tokens a recurring concern. Stolen keys can expose customer environments, enable unauthorised use of services or create significant costs.

Read the SecurityWeek coverage.

AI is also becoming a critical part of the defence

The same developments creating new risks are also giving security teams more powerful ways to protect their organisations. AI can help process large volumes of security information, identify patterns, detect unusual behaviour and prioritise potential threats.

Agentic systems can take this further by supporting multi-step investigations, gathering evidence and recommending or initiating defined responses. But autonomy must come with control. An agent with access to sensitive systems needs clearly defined permissions, limits on what it can change, appropriate human oversight and a record of the actions it takes.

“The next evolution of cybersecurity will not be defined by how many alerts an organisation generates, but by how intelligently it can interpret and act on them. Agentic AI introduces the ability to investigate, correlate and respond across interconnected systems. However, autonomy must be engineered, not assumed. The competitive advantage will come from combining machine intelligence with controlled permissions, human oversight and clearly defined accountability.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

Japan's government also announced a 10 billion yen cybersecurity response package, reported at approximately $63 million, including an expert team using AI to identify network weaknesses and support cyber response. It is another indication that AI-supported defence is becoming a strategic investment, not simply an experimental capability.

Read the Associated Press report on Japan's response.

Five questions every business leader should be asking

  • Where is our critical data? Do we understand where customer, financial, employee and commercially sensitive information is stored and processed?
  • Who and what has access? Can we identify which employees, applications, suppliers and AI agents can access important systems and information?
  • Can we recognise unusual behaviour? Do we have visibility across connected systems, and can suspicious activity be identified before it escalates?
  • Are our AI agents properly governed? Are permissions restricted to what each agent needs, with clear boundaries, monitoring and human approval where appropriate?
  • Can we respond quickly? If an employee account, supplier connection or AI workflow is compromised, do we know how to isolate it, revoke access, investigate and recover?
The business lesson

AI adoption, data governance and cybersecurity can no longer be treated as separate conversations. They are becoming part of the same operating model.

Understanding the systems before automating them

AI adoption is accelerating, but implementing technology without understanding the business environment around it creates unnecessary exposure. Before automating processes or deploying agents, organisations need visibility into their operations, data, dependencies, access controls and existing vulnerabilities.

At Neural Horizons AI, this is central to our approach to AI strategy and implementation: understand the business problem, identify operational dependencies and establish the right foundations before introducing automation. The objective is not to slow down AI adoption. It is to make sure it is commercially valuable, controlled and sustainable.

The organisations that succeed will not necessarily be those deploying the most AI. They will be the ones that understand what their AI can access, what it is authorised to do, how its actions are monitored and who remains accountable.

If you introduced an AI agent into your business tomorrow, would you know exactly what it could access, what it could do and how you would detect it if something went wrong?
